**Where we are ahead:** the only durable, single-file (no server, no Redis, no Postgres) background queue in pure Zig with lease/retry/DLQ, a durable id counter with crash-safe enqueue, per-partition FIFO under a priority override, scheduled visibility and injected wall and monotonic clocks so retries, backoff and lease expiry are testable under `kv.SimStorage`; `enqueue` returns only after fsync. **Where we are behind:** single process only (leases are in memory), no worker runtime (concurrency, graceful shutdown, handler registry) or web UI, no scheduler (a cron expression parser is here, the caller enqueues each next run); each is in *Backlog / deferred*. Also built: unique-key TTL (`unique_ttl_ns`, as Asynq's `Unique(ttl)`), weighted dispatch across partitions (`DequeueOptions.weights`, as Asynq's and Sidekiq's weighted queues), a cron expression parser (`Cron`), job cancel, dead-letter requeue, lease heartbeat (`extendLease`), unique jobs, `status`, lease `release`, `dequeue` partition exclusion.

## Design & invariants

- **Durable background-job queue over `kv`:** `enqueue` → `dequeue` (lease) → `ack`/`nack`, with
  retry+backoff, a dead-letter queue, per-partition FIFO ordering under a priority override, and
  scheduled visibility (`delay_ns`/`run_at`). Greenfield over `kv`; the partition-FIFO dispatch
  shape is original design work; Faktory/Sidekiq (lease/reserve, retry-with-backoff, dead-letter)
  and the `resilience`/`jwt` sibling clock-injection pattern are behavioral/design references only.
- **In-memory index over a point store.** `kv` is `put`/`get`/`delete` by key (plus a key listing, `Db.keys(prefix)`; no record scan, and the id-counter replay below does not use it); a
  queue must *enumerate* ready work, so jobqueue keeps its own index (`jobs`, the ready pair
  `pending`/`parts`, `leased`, `dlq`) and uses `kv` purely as the durable record of truth,
  rebuilt on `open`.
- **Dispatch = two ordered structures, not one heap.** A ready job is not necessarily *visible*:
  a `delay_ns`/`run_at` job, or one serving a `nack` backoff, is ready but scheduled. A single
  heap keyed by (priority, id) cannot express that — its top may be the invisible job, and
  popping past it to find a visible one destroys the ordering. So the ready set is split:
  `pending`, one min-heap on (`run_at_ns`, id) holding every job whose schedule has not been
  observed to arrive, and `parts`, one max-heap per partition on (priority desc, id asc) holding
  the jobs visible now. `dequeue` drains the due prefix of `pending` into the partition heaps,
  then takes the best partition-heap top — O(1) partition lookup under a `.partition` filter,
  O(partitions) without, plus O(log n) for the pop. Every job (fresh, recovered or requeued)
  enters through `pending`, so exactly one structure needs capacity reserved before the durable
  write. Visibility is still decided per `dequeue` call, never cached: the wall clock may step
  backwards, and a job that migrated but is no longer due is demoted back to `pending`.
- **Ordering: strict priority, ties FIFO by id — deliberately starvable.** A partition is a FIFO
  grouping key and a dispatch filter, not a fair-share class; an unfiltered `dequeue` returns the
  globally best job, so unbounded high-priority work starves low-priority work. That is what a
  priority override means, and it is not a regression (v1's linear scan chose identically). The
  mitigation available to callers is a per-partition worker (`dequeue(.{ .partition = … })`),
  which is fully isolated from other partitions' load.
- **Durable monotonic id counter, no scan needed for enumeration.** Each job is keyed `j/<id>` from
  a durable counter at `m/next_id`. `enqueue` writes the job record (fsync'd by `kv`) **then** bumps
  the counter (also fsync'd): a returned `enqueue` is fully durable, and a crash between the two
  writes leaves an orphan record the counter never references (safe, not double-counted).
  Recovery is a bounded replay — for `id in 1..next_id`, `kv.get(j/<id>)`: null (acked ⇒
  `kv.delete`d) is skipped, present is decoded and re-indexed.
- **Two injected clocks:** wall (`i64` ns, Unix epoch) drives the schedule (`run_at`, `delay_ns`,
  `nack` backoff visibility); monotonic (`u64` ns) drives lease expiry (a leased job is invisible
  until acked or its visibility timeout lapses). Both injectable for deterministic tests.
  `kv`'s `Storage` seam passes straight through (production: `kv.FsStorage`; tests: `kv.SimStorage`).
- **Concurrency:** single_owner — one owner drives the queue and the caller-driven maintenance
  sweep (`reapExpiredLeases`, like `kv`'s caller-driven `compact`); the in-memory index is not
  internally locked.

- **Operator tools.** `cancel(id)`: a ready, scheduled or dead job is deleted
  durably (`kv.delete`, as `ack`) and its unique key released; a leased one is
  `error.JobLeased` (the worker owns it until ack/nack/lapse). The dispatch heaps have no removal
  by id, so a cancelled ready job leaves a **tombstone** entry: `migrateDue` and `dequeue` drop an
  entry whose id is no longer in `jobs` (ids are never reused, so a tombstone cannot be mistaken
  for a live job); a scheduled tombstone sits in `pending` until its `run_at`. `requeueDead(id)`
  persists the job as ready (attempts reset to 0, or kept one short of the limit) at `run_at`
  (default now) before touching the index. `extendLease(lease, t)` sets the monotonic deadline to
  `now + t` for the current lease only (`StaleLease` otherwise). `status(id)` reads the index.
- **Lease release.** `release(lease, .{ .delay_ns })` hands a lease back without
  counting an attempt: the job returns to `pending` with its attempts, priority and id unchanged,
  never dead-letters, and keeps its `unique_key`. With `delay_ns == 0` it rejoins its partition
  heap at its old FIFO place at once; with a delay it is invisible until then, so newer jobs of the
  same partition can be dispatched before it (when it is due it sorts by its old id again). With `delay_ns > 0` the new `run_at` is persisted before the index changes (a
  storage error leaves the job leased and unchanged, as `expireLease` does); with 0 nothing is
  written, because the stored record already says what a reopen must see (ready, same attempts)
  and its `run_at` was due when it was dequeued. The lease epoch is bumped, so the released lease
  is `StaleLease` for `ack`/`nack`/`extendLease`/`release`; `validate` is shared, so a stale,
  reaped or forged lease gets the same error as everywhere else. *Reference survey (owner rule):*
  beanstalkd `release <id> <pri> <delay>` ("puts a reserved job back into the ready queue … when
  the job fails because of a transitory error"; counted in `releases`, not `timeouts`); River
  `JobSnooze(d)` ("will not increment the job's Attempt count … can be repeatedly snoozed without
  ever being discarded"); Celery `reject(requeue=True)`; BullMQ `moveToDelayed`; SQS
  `ChangeMessageVisibility` to 0 (SQS is the outlier: its receive count still grows). Majority:
  a (lease, delay) call that consumes no attempt; the name follows beanstalkd (and Laravel's
  `release($delay)`). Sidekiq/Asynq have no worker-side equivalent (a job re-enqueues itself).
- **Dequeue with exclusions.** `DequeueOptions.exclude` lists partitions to pass
  over: `bestReady` skips their heaps, so nothing of an excluded partition is leased, popped or
  changed (a tombstone at its top stays until a dequeue that does not exclude it). A `partition`
  filter that is excluded gives null. Empty = the plain dequeue (the loop over the list does not
  run). Cost: a linear scan of the list per partition heap considered, O(partitions × excluded)
  per dequeue, no allocation; a hash set was not worth it for the intended handful of keys. The
  slice is borrowed for the call. Why: a caller that keeps a per-partition backoff of its own
  (writebehind's retry wait) needs the best job of the OTHER partitions without leasing — and
  then releasing — every job of the waiting ones (an earlier design did that; a key whose wait
  lapsed between two of those dequeues was written past its own older, still-leased record).
  Peers: BullMQ, Asynq and Sidekiq select by queue name lists (a worker's queue set) rather
  than by exclusion; the closest is a consumer that subscribes to all queues but the paused ones
  (BullMQ `pause` per queue, Asynq `Pause(queue)`), which is what this expresses per call.
- **Unique jobs.** `EnqueueOptions.unique_key` (≤ `max_field_len`) is checked before anything is
  written; the key is held by the live job (ready, scheduled, leased, dead) and released by ack,
  cancel or `removeJob`. It is durable: a job with a key is written as a **version-2 record** (31
  fixed bytes with version 2, `unique_len` u32 at 31..35, the key after the payload); every other
  job is still version 1, so a store with no unique keys stays readable by older builds. `open`
  rebuilds the key index and refuses a store with two live jobs holding one key (`enqueue` never
  writes that). `decodeJob` accepts exactly what `encodeJob` writes: version 1 or 2, a v2 key
  non-empty, `max_attempts ≥ 1`, `attempts ≤ max_attempts`, a ready job below its limit — the
  rest is `CorruptRecord` (a dead record with `max_attempts` 0 would underflow in `requeueDead`).
- **Unique-key TTL.** `EnqueueOptions.unique_ttl_ns` (Asynq `Unique(ttl)`; 0 = held until ack/cancel, as
  before) releases the key that many wall ns after the enqueue while the job is still live: the next
  `enqueue` with the key is accepted and `findUnique` returns null. Lapse is decided lazily at
  `enqueue`/`findUnique`, never by a timer. A TTL'd job is a **version-3 record** (version 2 plus
  `unique_until_ns` i64 at 35..43, body from 43; `decodeJob` refuses a v3 record with a non-positive
  deadline); jobs without a TTL stay v1/v2, so older builds still read such a store. The `unique` index
  borrows the holder's key bytes, so a lapsed holder is dropped from the index before a new holder is
  inserted, and `removeJob` frees a key only when the index still names that job (ack/cancel of a
  lapsed job leaves the new holder alone). `open` does not index a lapsed key; two live records with one
  key are `CorruptRecord` unless the older one has a TTL (a wall clock that stepped back can leave both
  unexpired: the newer wins).
- **Weighted dispatch.** `DequeueOptions.weights` (a `[]PartitionWeight`, no `partition` filter):
  smooth weighted round-robin (nginx's algorithm) over the partitions that have a visible top, in
  place of "best global top". Peers: Asynq weighted queues and Sidekiq weighted queues both pick a
  queue by weight (randomly, in proportion); a deterministic scheme gives the same proportions and is
  testable. Priority then orders jobs only inside the chosen partition; a partition not listed weighs 1,
  weight 0 passes it over, ties in credit go to the older top. The credit is one `i64` on the
  partition's heap (no allocation, gone when the partition runs dry). Strict priority stays the default.
- **Cron expressions.** `Cron.parse` / `Cron.next(after_ns)` / `Cron.matches` (`src/cron.zig`): the
  five-field Vixie syntax (lists, ranges, steps, `?`, month and weekday names, weekday 7, the `@hourly`
  .. `@yearly` aliases), dom/dow ORed when both are restricted. Reference: Vixie cron, which Asynq's
  scheduler (robfig/cron), Sidekiq-cron and BullMQ's repeat options follow. UTC, minute resolution,
  null when no date matches. The result is meant for `EnqueueOptions.run_at`; the queue has no scheduler.
  Not offered: `@every <duration>` and a time-zone argument (robfig has both; compute the offset or
  use `delay_ns`).
- **Recovery ownership.** Every slot (`jobs`, unique index, pending/dlq) is reserved before a
  recovered job is indexed, so an allocation failure frees the job once.


## Threat model / limits

Not a security boundary — durability/correctness, not adversarial hardening:
- **At-least-once delivery, explicitly not exactly-once.** A lease is an in-memory, single-process
  reservation (`kv` has no cross-process lock); a crash re-exposes every un-acked job as ready on
  the next `open`. A stale lease (timeout lapsed, job reaped/re-leased, released) cannot
  `ack`/`nack`/`extendLease`/`release` — it gets `error.StaleLease`. The consumer must be idempotent;
  this module does not enforce that.
- **`max_payload` cap** (default 1 MiB) bounds per-job memory; large blobs should be referenced out
  of band (e.g. via `blobstore`), not inlined. `job_type`, `partition` and `unique_key` are capped
  at `max_field_len` (4096).
- **Damaged stored records** are refused with `error.CorruptRecord` (or decode to a job that keeps
  every invariant), never a panic; `open` refuses a store that holds two live jobs with one
  `unique_key`.
- **Not provided:** cross-process leases and a scheduler thread (see *Backlog / deferred*),
  exactly-once and rate-limited dispatch (see *What is deliberately not done*).

## What is deliberately not done

- **Exactly-once delivery.** The queue is at-least-once; the idempotent consumer is the
  application's job (see *Threat model*).
- **Rate-limited dispatch inside the queue.** Compose the `ratelimit` module around `dequeue`.
- **A scheduler that fires cron entries.** `Cron` computes times; persisting a schedule and
  re-enqueueing from it is the worker runtime's part (Backlog), because it needs a thread and a
  handler registry. A caller enqueues the next run with `run_at = cron.next(now)` after each run.

## Verification

Run: `scripts/modtest jobqueue`; the example (`example/main.zig`) is built by
`zig build check-examples -Dmodule=jobqueue`. Class C (no wire format of its own), so the oracle is
a model, not a foreign implementation. The tests run on `kv.SimStorage` (the fault-injecting
fake) with fake wall and monotonic clocks, so crashes, lease expiry and the schedule are
deterministic.
- **Lifecycle and recovery:** enqueue -> lease -> ack (never reappears), the visibility timeout
  with `reapExpiredLeases` (attempt bumped), nack backoff and the exponential `computeBackoff`
  (capped, deterministic without jitter), dead-letter after `max_attempts`, crash recovery (acked
  stays gone, leased-not-acked returns ready, a dead job stays dead, no duplicate or loss, the
  orphan-record invariant of the durable id counter), the payload and field caps.
- **Dispatch order**, pinned specifically by: partition FIFO (the taskqueue-fold oracle),
  priority within one partition, a high job ahead of an earlier low, the FIFO tiebreak among
  equals, cross-partition independence (an all-`critical` partition must not reorder another
  partition's FIFO), deterministic FIFO among equal priorities across partitions, a `critical` job
  that is not returned before its schedule even though it outranks everything visible, that same
  job winning once due, and a wall-clock step backwards re-hiding an already-eligible job. The
  `run_at` boundary is pinned from both sides at nanosecond granularity (invisible at `run_at - 1`,
  dispatched at `run_at`, re-hidden by a one-nanosecond step back), because the migration gate and
  the pop-time re-check both compare at nanosecond granularity.
- **Operator tools and later additions:** `cancel` in every state (including the tombstone skipped
  by `dequeue`, a scheduled one dropped at its time, durable across a crash), `requeueDead` with
  and without a reset, the heartbeat boundary (an extended deadline is inclusive; a reaped lease
  can neither extend nor ack), unique keys across ack / cancel / dead / reopen, `status`,
  `release` (no attempt counted, never dead-letters, keeps its FIFO place without a delay, a stale
  released lease, a delay survives a reopen and without one nothing is written, the unique key stays
  held), `DequeueOptions.exclude` (other partitions served in order, an excluded one untouched,
  an excluded tombstone stays put), and records: keyless jobs are still version-1, `decodeJob`
  refuses what the module never writes (a keyless v2 record, a dead job with `max_attempts` 0),
  `open` refuses two live jobs with one key.
- **TTL, weights, cron:** unique-key TTL (lapse at exactly the deadline, across a reopen, an old lapsed holder cancelled without freeing the new holder's key, v3 record only with a key), weighted dispatch (3:1 over a run, priority ignored across partitions, unlisted = 1, weight 0 passed over), and `Cron` (common expressions, the dom/dow OR rule, leap day and impossible dates, lists/ranges/steps, refusals).
- **Seeded sweeps:** a damaged-record sweep over `decodeJob` (v1 and v2 encodings with length
  fields, version, state/priority, attempt counts, truncation and random bytes damaged: always
  `CorruptRecord` or a job that keeps the invariants, with floors on how many inputs decode and how
  many are refused), and a model sweep (many seeds of random operations: enqueue with keys, delays
  and priorities, dequeue with and without an exclusion list, ack, nack, extend, reap with clock
  moves, cancel, `requeueDead`, `release` with a random delay, crash-and-reopen) that compares
  every job's status and all the counts with a model after every step.
- **Fuzz:** the card records no fuzz obligation (the seeded sweeps above are ordinary tests, not an
  `JOBQUEUE_FUZZ` driver).
- **Audit:** the card's `**Audit:**` line is the current score, cumulative over the last
  whole-module mutation run and the delta runs after it.
- **Dependents:** `writebehind` builds on this module; run its modtest after a change here.

## Backlog / deferred

None open.

## Roadmap

- **Durable, cross-process leases.** Leases live in memory (single-process worker model); several
  worker processes would need a shared queue and a cross-process lock in `kv`. Effort: large. Size: a shared queue with a cross-process lock in `kv`, weeks.
- **Worker runtime** (concurrency, graceful shutdown, handler dispatch by job type, a scheduler that
  fires `Cron` entries, a background lease-sweep / `kv.compact` thread with a trigger policy):
  Sidekiq and Asynq ship it; here the caller writes the loop and drives `reapExpiredLeases` and
  `kv.compact` (`workerpool` exists as a sibling). A separate module composing `jobqueue` +
  `workerpool`. Effort: large. Size: a separate module composing `jobqueue` and `workerpool` (scheduler, graceful shutdown, handler dispatch), weeks.

## Anchoring

**Anchor grade:** class C · oracle n/a

- **Class C** — internal algorithm or data structure — no outside exists, so correctness is defined by invariants or a brute-force reference. Not anchor debt.
- **Oracle n/a** — class C/D carries no anchor debt, so there is no oracle grade to give.

**What the tests actually contain.** internal partition-FIFO dispatch queue; original design, no wire format
